learning.title: Read the isolation default on the route that writes the row you order by
learning.trigger: A test or query expects rows in `created_at desc` order, `created_at` defaults to `now()`, and the rows are written by more than one request, handler or statement.
learning.symptom: An expectation about ordering is repeatedly wrong in ways that each look like a different bug. Every diagnosis names a plausible mechanism - tie-break, UUID byte order, positional index, string comparison - and each fix moves the failure to the next one instead of removing it. The runs are stable, so the assertion looks correct and the argument is about why the system misbehaves.
learning.rule: `now()` is the TRANSACTION's start, not the statement's and not the request's. Two rows share a `created_at` only if they were written inside one transaction. Whether ids, tie-breaks or byte order decide anything therefore depends on the transaction boundary of the route that creates the rows - read it before reasoning about the ordering at all.

The default isolation and transaction shape are not on the route that does the reading. Find the writer. A route that does not set `transactionIsolation` gets the default, and each request to it is its own transaction, so its rows get distinct `now()` values and any tie-break you wrote never runs.

When several diagnoses of one assertion have each named a different plausible mechanism, stop diagnosing and read the source that creates the data. Five confident theories in a row were all downstream of one unread default.
learning.evidence: PR 540, the same assertion red five times before it was right. Five causes in order: a positional index; the ticket tie-break; the paging order; an inverted link ternary; and finally the real one - each `/links` POST is its own transaction (`ticket-actions.ts` registers the route without `transactionIsolation`; `authority-postgres.ts:584` defaults to `ReadCommitted`), so the two links have strictly different `created_at` values, `created_at desc` decides alone, and the `id desc` tie-break never ran. Every derivation up to that point answered "which id is larger", a question the read does not ask. The first four causes were all downstream: nobody had read the isolation default on the route that creates the row being ordered. Fixed in `985e34d1d`.
